chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, all together from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Jameela, from Humran, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who bequeathed at the time of his death, 'Free so-and-so, and so-and-so, and so-and-so, and so-and-so, and so-and-so.' I looked into his one-third share, but it did not reach the price/value of the five slaves whom he ordered to be freed. He said: 'Look at those he named and begin by freeing them. Appraise them and look at his one-third share, so free from it the first one, then the second, then the third, then the fourth, then the fifth. If the one-third is insufficient for what he named, stop, for the one he named last is freed after the one-third is exhausted, which is what he does not own, so that is not permissible for him.'

key_terms.ثُلُثِهِ: His one-third share (of the estate for bequests)

ai.seo_question: How is the one-third estate distributed when freeing multiple slaves if the funds are insufficient?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the principle of proportional execution in bequests, where the Imam clarifies that emancipation follows the chronological order of naming rather than equal distribution. This ruling ensures that the first named slaves are fully freed from the available one-third share, while the last named slave bears the shortfall, reflecting the Shia juristic view that the testator's explicit sequence dictates priority. It highlights the practical application of the 'one-third' limit in Islamic inheritance law when specific assets (slaves) exceed the disposable estate portion.
